summary:
AstroCraft is a browser-based mission design game that lets players act as a spacecraft architecture team. They pick a NASA-inspired scenario (Moon south pole ice prospecting, Mars surface geology, asteroid survey, or Earth observation), choose a launch vehicle, instruments, power, communications and trajectory, and check launch readiness. They then simulate the mission, where random events like solar flares, dust storms and budget cuts test the design, and review a scored debrief. It runs solo or in teams of up to four, and needs no installation.

The game makes real engineering trade-offs visible and hands-on. Players see how adding instruments raises mass, power draw and data volume, how solar power falls with distance from the Sun, and how communications and storage limit science return. Its data, logic and interface layers are separate, so educators and developers can easily add scenarios and parts.

This matters because space missions succeed through system-level thinking. AstroCraft builds that skill in students and the public, and it makes mission design approachable and engaging.
details: What it does and how it works AstroCraft is a single-page browser game in which players design a space mission. They choose a scenario, then build an architecture: spacecraft, science instruments, launch vehicle, power system, communications and trajectory. A Validate step runs a launch readiness check that shows pass or fail margins for mass, power, communications and reliability, with explanations. Simulate then runs the mission, and randomized events such as solar flares, dust storms, antenna drift and budget cuts add pressure. A debrief shows a score, an event timeline and explanations of what drove the result, so players can redesign and compare. It has solo and 1-4 player team modes with roles (Mission Director, Systems Engineer, Science Lead, Flight Operations), a sandbox mode, a short tutorial and educational concept cards. Benefits Players learn by doing, with immediate feedback instead of lectures. There is no install, and it runs by opening index.html. There is no single perfect build. Scoring rewards science return, efficient resource use and robustness, so different strategies can win. Team mode encourages discussion about which subsystem caused a result. Intended impact AstroCraft aims to build systems-engineering thinking in students and the public. The lesson is that mission success depends on balancing cost, mass, power, data and reliability together, not on one component. Educators and developers can also extend it with their own scenarios. Tools and technology HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with a responsive layout and no frameworks or packages Optional local server (python -m http.server) for testing A seeded pseudo-random generator, so simulations are deterministic and testable Three layers: data.js (scenarios, parts, events, education), gameLogic.js (pure calculation functions) and app.js with index.html and styles.css (state and UI) Creativity Space engineering is framed as a game with consequences, not a quiz. Random events create a second layer of pressure after the design is done. Team roles mirror real mission teams. The content is modular, so new missions, hardware and events can be added by editing data only. Factors the team considered Realism versus playability: the values are NASA/JPL-inspired but simplified, and tuned to teach trade-offs rather than match real hardware specs. Accessibility: no installation, a short tutorial and a quick start in about 30 seconds. Variety of difficulty: scenarios range from Low (Earth observation) to High (Mars). Extensibility and testability: separated layers and deterministic logic. Real constraints: solar power falloff with distance, signal delay, storage limits and data bottlenecks.
